title: Non-coal mineral concessions in India: the auction regime, the blocks, and the failure rate

method.question: Which non-coal mineral concessions has the Indian state auctioned since the 2015 regime change, to whom, at what price, and how often did the auction fail?
method.whatCounts: A mineral block for which a mining lease, prospecting licence-cum-mining lease or composite licence was granted through auction under the MMDR Act, 1957 as amended in 2015 and 2023. Coal, lignite, offshore minerals, minor minerals and Exploration Licences are all excluded, each for a stated reason in the rejected array.
method.theBidParameter: There are no rupee contract values in this domain and their absence is not a hole. Under the Mineral (Auction) Rules the bidder quotes a PERCENTAGE OF THE VALUE OF MINERAL DISPATCHED, payable monthly to the State Government on top of royalty, the District Mineral Foundation levy and the National Mineral Exploration Trust levy. Every 'premium' or 'final price offer' in this file is that percentage. It can and does exceed 100%.
registersUsed: Ministry of Mines, 'Successful Auction Details as on 04.10.2019' - 70 blocks, the richest single artefact in this domain, recovered from the Internet Archive because the live URL 404s.
MSTC Limited mineral auction result table (mlcln) - 181 state blocks and 22 central critical-mineral blocks concluded in FY2025-26 and FY2026-27, harvested programmatically rather than transcribed.
PIB block-wise tables for critical-mineral tranches IV and V - 20 blocks.
Trade-press reporting of the tranche I winners - 5 records, one with a block name.
Ministry of Mines Annual Report 2025-26 for the state-wise and mineral-wise totals to 31.12.2025.
method.transcriptionPolicy: The 70 rows of the 2019 register were transcribed by hand from the extracted PDF text and their mineral, state and winner tallies were checked back against the source's own totals. Every other block record was generated programmatically from the fetched HTML, so it cannot contain a transcription error. Where the source itself is defective - a blank revenue cell, an area printed as '13053 ha', a premium of 3,390.05% - the value is recorded as printed and carries a dataQualityFlag. Nothing was silently corrected.
method.namePolicy: Winner names are recorded exactly as printed in `winnerAsPrinted`. Normalisation for the concentration statistics is declared in full in denominators.firstRegisterWinners, including which merges were made, on what basis, and which merges were REFUSED on the date test. Both the raw and the normalised distributions are published so the effect of every merge is visible.
method.whatThisIsNot: Not a census. 298 block records against 592 blocks auctioned since 2015; the coverage is two well-documented windows (2016-2019 and 2025-2026) with a five-year hole between them. Any concentration figure computed from these blocks is a figure about these blocks.

regime.instrument: The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2015
regime.gazetteCitation: Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II Section 1, No. 13, New Delhi, Friday, March 27, 2015 / Chaitra 6, 1937 (Saka)
regime.commencementNote: Section 1(2): 'It shall be deemed to have come into force on the 12th day of January, 2015' - the date of the MMDR Amendment Ordinance that the Act replaced. Assent, publication and deemed commencement are three different dates and are recorded separately here because the auction cut-off runs from the deemed commencement, not the assent.
regime.whatChanged: Replaced discretionary, first-come-first-served grant of mineral concessions with mandatory competitive auction. New section 10A(1) made ALL applications received before commencement ineligible, subject to the saving clauses in 10A(2). New section 10B(4) required the State Government to select the mining-lease holder for a notified mineral 'through auction by a method of competitive bidding, including e-auction'. New section 10B(2) and substituted section 11 extended the same auction route to the prospecting licence-cum-mining lease, the composite licence, defined in the new section 3(ga) as 'a two stage concession granted for the purpose of undertaking prospecting operations followed by mining operations'. New section 8A(4) provides that on expiry of a lease period the lease 'shall be put up for auction as per the procedure specified in this Act'.
regime.otherProvisions: Section 8A set a uniform 50-year lease term for non-coal, non-atomic minerals; section 9B created the District Mineral Foundation; section 9C created the National Mineral Exploration Trust at 2% of royalty; section 3(ea) defined 'notified minerals' as those in the new Fourth Schedule; a Special Court was provided for under section 30B.
regime.bidParameter: Percentage of the value of mineral dispatched, quoted by the bidder and payable monthly to the State Government in addition to royalty, DMF and NMET. This is why mineral-auction outcomes have no rupee contract value: the price is a percentage, not an amount.

regime.instrument: Mineral (Auction) Rules, 2015, made under section 13 of the MMDR Act
regime.commencementNote: NOT READ IN THIS PASS. The rules are cited by every source used here and are the instrument that sets the two-stage ascending forward auction, the minimum-three-technically-qualified-bidders condition and the annulment power, but the gazette text of the 2015 rules and their 2017/2024/2025/2026 amendments was not retrieved. Everything this file says about the rules is therefore taken from ministry and press descriptions of them, not from the rules.
regime.whatChanged: Per the CSEP note and PIB releases: online e-auction only; two-stage ascending forward auction where the highest first-stage offer becomes the second-stage floor; upfront payment of 0.50% of the value of estimated resources under section 11; performance security of 0.50%; and a reserve price expressed as a minimum percentage of the value of mineral dispatched, typically 5% for limestone and 35% for the Karnataka iron-ore leases.
regime.otherProvisions: Sub-rules 10 and 11(b) of rule 9 are the second-attempt provision under which failed blocks are re-offered; the Ministry of Mines cited them by number when launching Tranche III.
regime.bidParameter: Highest percentage of the value of mineral dispatched.

regime.instrument: The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2023
regime.gazetteCitation: Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II Section 1, No. 19, New Delhi, Wednesday, August 9, 2023 / Sravana 18, 1945 (Saka)
regime.commencementNote: Section 1(2) of the Act leaves commencement to notification. The Ministry of Mines, the Minister's Rajya Sabha reply and the Ministry's own Annual Report 2025-26 all give the effective date as 17 August 2023. The commencement notification itself was not retrieved, so the 17 August date is documented by three ministry statements rather than by the notification.
regime.whatChanged: Inserted section 11D: 'Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, the Central Government shall, for the purpose of granting mining lease or composite licence in any area in respect of any mineral specified in the Part D of the First Schedule, select, through auction by method of competitive bidding, including e-auction, a preferred bidder...'. Section 11D(3) provides that royalty, dead rent and the auction premium accrue to the State Government as if the State had run the auction. Also inserted section 10BA creating the Exploration Licence for the 29 minerals in the new Seventh Schedule, and omitted six minerals (lithium, beryllium, titanium, niobium, tantalum, zirconium bearing minerals) from the Part B atomic-minerals list, opening them to the private sector.
regime.otherProvisions: Part D of the First Schedule, inserted by section 20(iii), lists exactly 24 critical and strategic minerals: beryl and other beryllium bearing minerals; cadmium bearing minerals; cobalt bearing minerals; gallium bearing minerals; glauconite; graphite; indium bearing minerals; lithium bearing minerals; molybdenum bearing minerals; nickel bearing minerals; niobium bearing minerals; phosphate (without uranium); platinum group of elements bearing minerals; potash; minerals of the 'rare earths' group not containing Uranium and Thorium; rhenium bearing minerals; selenium bearing minerals; tantalum bearing minerals; tellurium bearing minerals; tin bearing minerals; titanium bearing minerals and ores (ilmenite, rutile and leucoxene); tungsten bearing minerals; vanadium bearing minerals; zirconium bearing minerals and ores including zircon.
regime.bidParameter: Highest percentage of the value of mineral dispatched, same parameter as the state auctions; the revenue accrues to the State even though the Centre runs the auction.

tranches.note: The first auction ever held under section 11D. All 20 block names are in Annexure I of the 5 Feb 2024 Rajya Sabha reply. More than 180 tender documents were purchased and 'more than 50 bids' were received; Swarajya reports 56 physical and 56 online bids for 18 of the 20 blocks, i.e. two blocks drew no bid at all. Six blocks were awarded and the winners announced on 24 June 2024 alongside the Tranche IV launch. THE THREE COUNTS DO NOT CLOSE: 20 offered minus 6 awarded leaves 14 unawarded, but the wire report of the annulment notices counts 13 annulled in this tranche. One block is unaccounted for in the sources opened and is recorded here as unreconciled rather than assigned. Named bidders in the round included Vedanta, Coal India, NLC India, Shree Cement, Orient Cements, Ola Electric, Dalmia Group, Rungta Group and Jindal Power - none of whom won a block in it.

denominators.note: Every rate in this file is published with the denominator it was computed on. Three different denominators are in circulation for the same programme and they give answers that differ by 18 percentage points; the ministry publishes the most flattering one.

criticalMineralAuction.windowCovered: Tranche I (NIT 29 Nov 2023) through Tranche VII (results 16-23 Jun 2026). Tranche VIII, launched 15 Jul 2026 with bids closing 21 Sep 2026, is excluded because it has no result.
criticalMineralAuction.blockOfferingsNote: One block offered in three tranches counts three times. This equals the ministry's own count of Notice Inviting Tenders: the Annual Report 2025-26 states 104 NITs for tranches I-VI, and 20+18+7+21+15+23 = 104 exactly. Adding Tranche VII's 19 gives 123.
criticalMineralAuction.uniqueBlocksOfferedNote: The ministry's figure, stated as '56 of the 88 unique mineral blocks offered so far' after Tranche VII. It reconciles with the earlier published unique-block counts: 48 after Tranche IV, 55 after Tranche V, 76 after Tranche VI (Annual Report 2025-26), 88 after Tranche VII.
criticalMineralAuction.unreconciledNote: 20 blocks were offered in Tranche I, 6 were awarded and the wire report of the annulment notices counts 13 annulled there, leaving one block unaccounted for. Swarajya, reporting the Tranche I results, says 14 of the 20 remained unawarded, which would close the arithmetic - so the likeliest reading is that one Tranche I block failed outside the 13-block annulment notice. Recorded as unreconciled rather than assigned.
criticalMineralAuction.theGap: The ministry's published success rate is 63.64% (56 of 88 unique blocks). The rate per auction actually held is 45.53% (56 of 123 offerings). The difference is the second-attempt machinery: a block re-offered until it sells is counted once in the numerator and once in the denominator, so re-auctions are invisible in the headline. The annulment rate on offerings is 53.66%. Both numbers are correct; only one is published.
criticalMineralAuction.annulmentGrounds: Two grounds appear in the annulment notices: nil bids, and fewer than three technically qualified bidders. Tranche VII: 2 nil-bid, 7 sub-three-bidder. Tranche VI: 5 nil-bid, 5 sub-three-bidder, plus one further block (Beku Rare Metal, West Bengal) on unstated grounds. Tranche II: 5 of the 14 received no bids. Tranche I: 2 of the 20 blocks received no bid at all. The three-qualified-bidder floor is a rule of the auction, not a market outcome - a block with two serious bidders is annulled by design.

baseRates.claim: Does 'this company won more than one mineral block' single anybody out?
baseRates.denominatorLabel: distinct winners in the Ministry of Mines register of the first 70 non-coal blocks (2016-2019), after name normalisation

comparators.set: MSTC state blocks, FY2025-26 and FY2026-27 (183 blocks)

baseRates.verdict: WEAK to MODERATE, and it depends which window you pick: 41.0% of winners in the 2016-19 register took more than one block, 29.1% in the recent state window, 30.8% in the central critical-mineral rounds. Under the evidence-tiering rule this is a 10-40%/40-80% borderline - usable only with a control group and an effect size, never on its own. 'Company X won two blocks' is not a finding.
baseRates.innocentReading: Mineral blocks are auctioned in clusters: one NIT typically covers several adjacent leases in the same district, and a bidder that has done the geology and mobilised a bid team for one will bid for its neighbours. Ten of the fourteen Karnataka iron-ore leases in the 2019 register came from two NITs covering the same Bellary belt on the same days.

baseRates.claim: How concentrated is the winner side, really?
baseRates.denominatorLabel: the 70 blocks in the Ministry of Mines register as on 04.10.2019

comparators.set: top three winners combined, MSTC state window
top three winners combined, central critical minerals

baseRates.verdict: LOW BY THE STANDARDS OF INDIAN PROCUREMENT. The most concentrated of the three windows has a top winner on 12.86% of blocks and a Herfindahl of 432.7 on block counts. Compare the ICIP central-tenders file, where one bidder took 6 of 6 airports in the 2018-19 AAI round and the top telecom bidder took 58.65% of spectrum value. Mineral auctions are a long-tail market: 23 of 39 winners in the 2019 register, 73 of 103 in the recent state window and 18 of 26 in the central critical-mineral rounds took exactly one block. Any story about capture has to explain the tail, not just the head.
baseRates.innocentReading: Mining leases are geographically fixed and mostly captive. A cement plant bids for the limestone under it and for nothing else; there is no reason for a national player to sweep a market it cannot transport. The long tail is what a geography-bound auction should look like.

baseRates.denominatorLabel: limestone blocks in the 2019 ministry register

baseRates.verdict: NON-DISCRIMINATING. At this rate the fact carries no information: of course the limestone goes to cement and the iron ore to steel. Publishing 'cement company wins limestone block' as a finding would be base-rate neglect in its purest form. The interesting question is the reverse one - who wins a block WITHOUT a downstream plant, and at what price - and the CSEP analysis answers it: the single merchant limestone bidder in the register won at 25.6% while captive bidders averaged 47%, and the single merchant iron-ore bidder won at 39.1% against a captive average near 87%.
baseRates.innocentReading: This is what end-use reservation is designed to produce. The Mineral (Auction) Rules permitted blocks to be reserved for a specified end use, and a captive bidder can rationally pay more because it is buying supply security for a plant, not margin on ore.

baseRates.claim: How often does the winning premium exceed 100% of the value of the mineral dispatched - i.e. the winner has contracted to pay the state more than the ore is nominally worth, before royalty?
baseRates.denominatorLabel: blocks in the 2019 ministry register with a published winning premium

comparators.set: MSTC state window (181 blocks with a premium)
central critical minerals, tranches IV-VII (42 blocks)

baseRates.verdict: MODERATE and rising. Roughly a fifth of the first 70 blocks cleared above 100%; the recent state window is lower, and the central critical-mineral rounds are much higher and much more extreme - a 835.00% bid on the Kanaital graphite block in Odisha and 752.05% on Ponchi graphite in Jharkhand. Above 100% the premium alone exceeds the notified value of the mineral, so either the bidder expects the resource or the price to be far larger than the government's estimate, or the bid is not primarily about the ore.
baseRates.innocentReading: Three benign readings, all live. (a) The Indian Bureau of Mines average sale price used to value the resource can be well below the price a producer actually realises for a graded or beneficiated product. (b) A composite licence is a bet on exploration finding more than the G3/G4 estimate, so a high percentage on a small notified base can be rational. (c) The premium is paid on mineral actually dispatched: a bidder who never mines pays nothing, so an aggressive bid is a cheap option. This last reading is directly supported by the operationalisation figure - only 82 of 592 auctioned blocks had started production at 31.12.2025.

baseRates.claim: How much of the central critical-mineral award set went to state-owned or state-linked bidders?

baseRates.claim: Is the critical-mineral programme failing at a rate that distinguishes it from the rest of the mineral auction regime?

comparators.set: state major-mineral auctions, FY2022-23 to 07.06.2022 (the only state annulment count sourced)
comparators.denominatorLabel: blocks whose auction had concluded one way or the other by that date

comparators.set: commercial coal mine auctions, latest round reported in the ICIP central-tenders file
comparators.note: 8 of 23 blocks drew bids - a 65% failure rate on a far more mature commodity. Recorded as context only; the coal auction runs under a different ministry, a different bid parameter and a different rulebook, and this file does not import its numbers.

baseRates.verdict: YES, but less dramatically than the raw gap suggests, and the right control matters. 53.66% of critical-mineral offerings were annulled against 31.9% of concluded state major-mineral outcomes in the one state snapshot available. But the state snapshot covers nine weeks, the commodity mix is completely different, and the state figure counts a block once per attempt too. The defensible statement is narrow: more than half of all critical-mineral auction attempts since November 2023 ended in annulment, and the two published grounds are nil bids and fewer than three technically qualified bidders.
baseRates.innocentReading: These are mostly greenfield composite licences on G3/G4 exploration in commodities with no domestic processing industry, no price discovery and no established buyer. A bidder is being asked to fund exploration for a mineral it cannot currently sell in India. A high failure rate is what an immature market looks like, and the three-qualified-bidder floor guarantees that thin interest becomes annulment rather than a low price. The government's own remedy has been procedural - shorter post-auction timelines, insurance surety bonds in place of bank guarantees, refund of bid security where an annulment is not the bidder's fault - which is consistent with reading the problem as participation, not integrity.

gaps: NO BLOCK-WISE RESULT DOCUMENT EXISTS FOR FIVE OF THE SEVEN CONCLUDED CRITICAL-MINERAL TRANCHES. PIB published a block-wise table with preferred bidders and premiums for Tranche IV (PRID 2071441 and 2077889) and Tranche V (PRID 2131723) and for no other tranche. Tranche VI and VII block-level results survive ONLY on the MSTC e-auction result table, which this file harvested; Tranche I results were announced at an event and reported by trade press with only one of six blocks named; Tranche II and Tranche III block-level results were not found anywhere. For a programme the government describes as central to national security, five of seven result sets are press releases or platform tables rather than result documents.

THE ANNULMENT NOTICES THEMSELVES WERE NOT RETRIEVED. Every per-tranche annulment count in this file (13 / 14 / 3 / 11 / 5 / 11 / 9) comes from a Press Trust of India wire report of 5 July 2026 that quotes the notices, not from the notices. The Ministry of Mines publishes annulment notices on MSTC and its own site; neither was reachable in a fetchable form for the historic tranches. These figures are therefore `reported`, not `documented`, and the whole annulment analysis in this file rests on one wire story plus one earlier wire story for Tranche VI.

THERE IS NO OFFICIAL CUMULATIVE ANNULMENT NUMBER ANYWHERE. The Ministry of Mines publishes blocks auctioned, in every release, in every annual report, on every dashboard. It does not publish blocks annulled. The 66 in this file had to be assembled from a newspaper's summary of seven separate notices. THE ABSENCE IS THE FINDING: the denominator that would let anyone compute a failure rate is the one number the programme does not report.

TRANCHE I DOES NOT RECONCILE. 20 blocks offered, 6 awarded, 13 annulled per the wire report - one block unaccounted for. Swarajya's contemporaneous report says 14 of 20 went unawarded, which would close it. Recorded as an unreconciled residual and not assigned.

TRANCHE II AND TRANCHE III SUCCESS COUNTS ARE DERIVED, NOT STATED. 4 and 4 are inferred from the ministry's own cumulative figure of 14 successful blocks at 31 July 2024 minus Tranche I's 6, split between the two tranches using their published annulment counts. No source states either number directly. If either published annulment count is wrong, both derived figures move.

NUMBER OF BIDDERS PER BLOCK EXISTS FOR 70 BLOCKS AND FOR NOTHING SINCE. The 2019 ministry register has a 'Quote received' column and it is the most analytically valuable field in this file - it is what would let anyone test whether high premiums come from thick or thin competition. Neither MSTC nor PIB nor the annual report publishes bidder counts. 46 of the 70 register rows carry one; 252 of the 298 block records in this file have quotesReceived: null.

MSTC RETAINS ONLY FY2025-26 ONWARDS. The one working machine-readable result source has no archive before April 2025. Between the ministry's last block-level register (04.10.2019, recovered from the Internet Archive) and April 2025 there is a five-and-a-half-year hole in the block-level record covering roughly 350 of the 592 auctions. Nothing found in this pass fills it.

THE MINISTRY'S OWN DASHBOARD IS UNFETCHABLE AND ITS HISTORIC FILES HAVE BEEN DELETED. mines.gov.in/webportal is an Angular app returning an identical 5,860-byte skeleton for every content URL; its data API (POST /admin/api/ManageAuction/viewAll) returns HTTP 500. The writereaddata PDFs that carried block-level detail up to 2022 now return 404 on the live site and exist only in the Internet Archive. Machine-readable public access to this record has gone backwards since 2019.

TEN STATE MINING DIRECTORATES COULD NOT BE REACHED FROM THIS ENVIRONMENT: Odisha, Karnataka, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh, over two network paths, by connection refusal or DNS failure. This is a statement about our access and NOT a finding that those states publish nothing. What it does establish is that the record is not retrievable by an ordinary automated request from outside India.

AREA AND RESERVE ESTIMATES EXIST FOR 70 OF 298 BLOCK RECORDS. Only the 2019 ministry register carries them. MSTC's result table has no mineral, area or reserve column; the PIB tranche tables have no area or reserve. So for every block auctioned since 2019 this file can say who won and at what percentage, but not how much mineral they won.

THE MINERAL (AUCTION) RULES, 2015 AND THEIR AMENDMENTS WERE NOT READ. The three-technically-qualified-bidder floor, the annulment power, the second-attempt provision in rule 9(10) and 9(11)(b), the upfront payment and the performance security are all described in this file from ministry and press accounts of the rules. The gazette text was not retrieved. The regime record for the rules is tiered `reported` accordingly.

THE COMMENCEMENT NOTIFICATION FOR THE MMDR AMENDMENT ACT, 2023 WAS NOT READ. The Act itself leaves commencement to notification; 17 August 2023 is stated by PIB, by the Minister in a Rajya Sabha reply and by the Ministry's Annual Report, but the notification was not opened.
TRANCHE VIII IS OPEN. Launched 15 July 2026, bids closed 21 September 2026, no result at this file's as-of date. Its 20 offerings are recorded but excluded from every rate.

THE MINISTRY CONTRADICTS ITSELF IN THREE PLACES AND NONE OF THEM IS RESOLVED HERE. (a) Annual Report Tables 3.4 and 3.5 give different year-row totals for 2017-18 (13 vs 14), 2019-20 (41 vs 43) and 2020-21 (16 vs 13), and both year-row series sum to 595 against a stated total of 592; the column totals both sum to 592 and are used. (b) The Year End Review says Madhya Pradesh auctioned 33 blocks in CY2025 in its narrative and 32 in its own table. (c) The Tranche VIII launch release says the eighth tranche takes 'the total number of critical mineral blocks offered to 88' when 88 was already the figure after Tranche VII three weeks earlier.

A MORE RECENT AND MORE GRANULAR PARLIAMENTARY ANSWER EXISTS AND IS NOT IN THIS FILE. A written reply by the Minister of State for Coal and Mines, reported 4 August 2026, gives 720 blocks auctioned since 2015 and 105 operationalised, with a state-wise table. The answer PDF could not be retrieved: sansad.in's question search is a client-rendered app and its PDF route requires a server-validated hash that cannot be constructed from the question number alone. The figures are therefore NOT recorded in this file even as `reported`, because only a journalist's transcription of them was seen. This is the single largest known gap in the totals section.

NO PER-BLOCK PREMIUM FOR TRANCHE I. Trade press reports the six Tranche I premiums as ranging from 13.05% to 400% but attributes only one to a block (Katghora, 76.05%). The other five are recorded with winner and state and a null premium.

THE ODISHA IRON-ORE ROUND OF JANUARY-FEBRUARY 2020 IS NOT IN THE BLOCK TABLE. Seventeen blocks were auctioned with a weighted average winning bid of about 106%, five of them below 100%.
